speaker: SPEAKER_04
text: Good evening. My name is Beth Robinson, and I'm here to speak against this ordinance. I have lived on these streets not once, but multiple times. I know what it's like to face long, cold, dark nights with nowhere safe to go. Those nights were terrifying. And I can tell you I would have never been able to rebuild my life back had I been cited, fined, or jailed simply for trying to survive. So I ask you directly, will this city also cite and fine the yuppies, the wealthy, for spreading out a blanket at a park, for laying down at a festival, for resting their head in public within city limits, or does this only apply to our unhoused neighbors? Even Charlottesville's staff have admitted there are not enough beds or shelter for everyone, yet this ordinance would punish people outside living outside while offering minimal safe, dignified alternatives without even designated camping areas, just punishment. Back in August of 2024, residents and advocates made it clear. We denounced the lock-em-up rhetoric. We asked for solutions rooted in dignity, not criminalization. Yet here we are debating whether survival should be treated as a crime. And make no mistake, even if the base violation is low level, it can quickly escalate. Citations turn into unpaid fines, fines into warrants, and warrants into arrest and criminal records. And once someone has that record, it causes it to nearly be impossible to get housing or a job. It traps people in the very cycle you claim you want to end. The unhoused are not strangers. They are our neighbors, and most don't even have access to basic sanitation, let alone a bed. Criminalization will not fix that. All it does is deepen suffering and punish people further from stability. You simply cannot punish people out of poverty and you cannot legislate away human need. I implore you to choose empathy. Thank you.
